subject: Biology
title: Predator-Prey Dynamics
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Predator-Prey Dynamics.

hook.text: When prey populations boom, predator populations follow. When prey crash, predators starve.

buildup.text: The lynx and snowshoe hare of Canada show this cycle—peaks and crashes roughly every ten years.

discovery.text: Predators keep prey from overgrazing. Without them, ecosystems become unbalanced.

twist.text: Prey drive predator evolution too. Faster rabbits force wolves to become faster hunters.

climax.text: This evolutionary arms race has shaped both predators and prey for millions of years.

punchline.text: Predator and prey dance in lockstep forever.

quiz.question: What happens to predator populations when prey numbers decline?

details.summary: Predator-prey dynamics describe the cyclical interactions between hunting and hunted species. Predator populations rise after prey increases, then fall as prey becomes scarce, creating linked oscillations. The classic lynx-hare cycle from Canadian fur records demonstrates this pattern.
details.whyItMatters: Predator-prey interactions regulate populations and maintain ecosystem balance. Removing top predators can cause prey population explosions that damage vegetation and destabilize entire ecosystems through trophic cascades.
takeaways: Predator and prey populations often cycle with a time lag between peaks
The Lotka-Volterra model mathematically describes predator-prey oscillations
Prey evolve defenses while predators evolve better hunting, creating arms races

faq.question: Why do predator and prey populations cycle?
faq.answer: When prey are abundant, predators thrive and multiply. Increased predation then depletes prey, causing predator starvation and decline. With fewer predators, prey recover, restarting the cycle. A time lag exists because predators respond to prey changes with a delay.

faq.question: What happens to ecosystems when top predators are removed?
faq.answer: Prey populations often explode, overgrazing vegetation and outcompeting other herbivores. This trophic cascade can transform entire landscapes. Removing wolves from parts of North America led to deer overpopulation, devastating forest understories.
